scenes.tts: Why do your mitochondria keep their own DNA? Because their ancestor was a free-living bacterium.
scenes.visual: 9:16. Frame one is already moving and already asks the question in the picture: on the dark ground one big PINK bean (6.0 wide x 3.2 tall, centre (0, 2.2)) with a double outline, and inside it a bright PINK ring of exactly 13 beads turning; a row of YELLOW blocks along its inner edge with a spark running. A large TEXT '?' (size 60) hangs beside the ring from the first frame. On 'your mitochondria' the label 'mitochondrion' (PINK, 40) writes above the bean. On 'own DNA' the ring flares and the label TRANSFORMS into 'its own DNA' (PINK, 44). On 'Because' the '?' fades and the picture pulls back fast: a tall BLUE cell outline (6.6 wide x 7.8 tall, centre (0, 1.2)) swings in around the bean, which settles to 3.6 x 1.9 at (0, 3.0), and a BLUE nucleus (solid circle r 1.2) with a blue bead ring sits low at (0, -1.0). On 'free-living bacterium' the bean's outline straightens into a straight PINK rod and holds for one full second with the label 'ancestor: a bacterium' (PINK, 40), then rounds back into the bean.
scenes.narration: Why do your mitochondria keep their own DNA? Because their ancestor was a free-living bacterium.

scenes.tts: Long ago, a larger cell somehow came to enclose a bacterium. You might expect a meal. But instead of being digested, the guest stayed.
scenes.visual: On 'Long ago' everything rewinds in one move: the bean straightens into a PINK rod (its bead ring swelling into a fuller ring of many small beads; never the 13-bead ring in the ancient guest) and rises out through the top of the blue outline to (0, 4.9); the nucleus's solid circle becomes a DASHED BLUE circle with a small GOLD '?' on its rim and the words 'nucleus yet?' (GOLD, 34) beside it (whether the host already had a nucleus is debated); its blue bead ring stays inside; the blue cell (now 6.2 x 5.4, centre (0, 0.4)) grows four thin arms at its top. Relative size only: the blue cell is the larger one; no scale. On 'somehow' two arms curl up and around the rod and draw it down inside to (0, 1.6); a GOLD '?' badge with 'how? one proposed way' (GOLD, 36) sits by the arms and fades when they close; the 'nucleus yet?' words fade at the same time, leaving the dashed circle and its small '?'. On 'a meal' a GREY ghost copy of the rod peels off to the lower right, crumbles to grey specks and fades: the fate that did not happen. On 'the guest stayed' the real PINK rod flares, its spark running, and 'it stayed' (PINK, 48) writes above it.
scenes.narration: Long ago, a larger cell somehow came to enclose a bacterium. You might expect a meal. But instead of being digested, the guest stayed.

scenes.tts: The traces are still there. Most mitochondria have two membranes and their own DNA. They even divide by pinching in two.
scenes.visual: The blue outline swells past the frame edges (a blue rim stays). Two plain PINK silhouettes stacked: 'mitochondrion' (bean, 5.6 x 2.6, centre (0, 3.4)) above and 'free relative' (rod, 5.2 x 2.2, centre (0, -0.6)) below, labels PINK 36 and TEXT 36. A GREEN link bar runs between them at the left. Each clue acts on BOTH at once and adds one green notch to the bar (three notches in all): on 'two membranes' both outlines split into two glowing lines; on 'own DNA' a PINK bead ring appears and turns in each; on 'pinching in two' both narrow at the waist in step and separate into two, each half keeping a ring. One clue word at a time (TEXT, 40) shows between the shapes and is replaced by the next: 'two membranes', 'own DNA', 'divide by pinching'. 'most mitochondria' (TEXT, 34) stays at the top. No ribosomes in this cut. No words such as 'the same way': these are resemblances.
scenes.narration: The traces are still there. Most mitochondria have two membranes and their own DNA. They even divide by pinching in two.

scenes.tts: Over time, many of its genes were lost, and others moved to the nucleus. But it kept a small genome of its own.
scenes.visual: The free relatives drop out of the bottom; one mitochondrion half drifts off the top and the other grows into a big PINK bean (5.6 x 2.8, centre (0, 3.4)) holding a ring of 40 countable beads, tagged 'schematic: not a gene count' (TEXT, 34); the BLUE cell outline returns around it, and the dashed circle below at (0, -1.2) draws SOLID (r 1.3) as its gold '?' drops away, the blue ring still inside. On 'were lost' 15 beads let go, turn GREY and fade. On 'moved to the nucleus' the label 'nucleus' (BLUE, 36) writes beside the blue circle and 12 beads FALL in a stream straight down into its ring and stay PINK there. On 'a small genome' the 13 beads left close into a tight ring that keeps turning. The 'schematic' tag stays on screen to the end of this scene. Labels never call the beads 'genes'.
scenes.narration: Over time, many of its genes were lost, and others moved to the nucleus. But it kept a small genome of its own.

scenes.tts: In humans, that DNA still codes for thirteen proteins. All thirteen help your cells get energy from food, using oxygen.
scenes.caption: In humans, that DNA still codes for 13 proteins. All 13 help your cells get energy from food, using oxygen.
scenes.visual: The picture pushes in on the bean so it fills the upper frame (6.4 x 3.4, centre (0, 2.4)); the nucleus leaves through the bottom. On 'thirteen proteins' the 13 beads flash in turn as a MONO counter runs 1 to 13 and stops; the 'schematic' tag fades only as the count starts; label '13 proteins' (PINK, 44). On 'All thirteen' each bead drops a PINK tile onto the row of YELLOW blocks on the bean's inner edge: the 13 PINK tiles slot in AMONG the YELLOW blocks, which stay (clearly more yellow blocks than pink tiles). Labels say 'proteins', never 'genes'. On 'energy' the row glows, a spark runs along it and YELLOW sparks rise from it in a stream; label 'energy from food' (YELLOW, 40). On 'using oxygen' the first RED dots marked 'O2' fall in from the top of the frame and land on the yellow row; each landing pops a YELLOW spark.
scenes.narration: In humans, that DNA still codes for 13 proteins. All 13 help your cells get energy from food, using oxygen.

scenes.tts: So every breath you take delivers oxygen to machinery inherited from that ancient guest. It moved in, and it never left.
scenes.visual: The counter and both labels fade; the bean and its glowing row stay large. On 'every breath' the fall of RED 'O2' dots thickens: they cross the blue rim and land one by one on the yellow row, each landing popping a YELLOW spark. On 'inherited' the label 'from the ancient guest' (PINK, 40) points at the row. On 'moved in' the ancient PINK rod flickers over the bean as a bright outline, then melts back into it. On 'never left' the bean pulses once, slowly. Oxygen keeps falling and sparks keep rising.
scenes.narration: So every breath you take delivers oxygen to machinery inherited from that ancient guest. It moved in, and it never left.

scenes.visual: End card over the still-living bean at 20% opacity. LINE (TITLE_FONT, 44, three short lines): 'Your mitochondria descend from a bacterium that moved in and never left.' Below it: 'Free at biochemistrypedia.com' (TEAL, 34). Everything above y -3.0.
